entries.60ebd04762143049524a7e8d9699ecc4efd53baf: <div sID="gen16149" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="31" osisID="Isa.31" sID="Isa.31"/> <div eID="gen16149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16150" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen16151" type="x-p"/> This chapter is an abridgment of the foregoing chapter; the heads of it are much the same. Here is, I. A woe to those who, when the Assyrian army invaded them, trusted to the Egyptians, and not to God, for succour, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1-Isa.31.3">ver. 1-3</reference>. II. Assurance given of the care God would take of Jerusalem in that time of danger and distress, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4-Isa.31.5">ver. 4, 5</reference>. III. A call to repentance and reformation, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6-Isa.31.7">ver. 6, 7</reference>. IV. A prediction of the fall of the Assyrian army, and the fright which the Assyrian king should thereby be put into, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8-Isa.31.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>.
entries.80e513c52e4eef13f8a2df8b24383e6a3b0efe16: <div eID="gen16151" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen16150" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Confidence in Egypt Reproved. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen16152" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help; and stay on horses, and trust in chariots, because <hi type="italic">they are</hi> many; and in horsemen, because they are very strong; but they look not unto the Holy One of Israel, neither seek the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> ! <hi type="super">2</hi> Yet he also <hi type="italic">is</hi> wise, and will bring evil, and will not call back his words: but will arise against the house of the evildoers, and against the help of them that work iniquity. <hi type="super">3</hi> Now the Egyptians <hi type="italic">are</hi> men, and not God; and their horses flesh, and not spirit. When the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> shall stretch out his hand, both he that helpeth shall fall, and he that is holpen shall fall down, and they all shall fail together. <hi type="super">4</hi> For thus hath the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> spoken unto me, Like as the lion and the young lion roaring on his prey, when a multitude of shepherds is called forth against him, <hi type="italic">he</hi> will not be afraid of their voice, nor abase himself for the noise of them: so shall the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts come down to fight for mount Zion, and for the hill thereof. <hi type="super">5</hi> As birds flying, so will the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> of hosts defend Jerusalem; defending also he will deliver <hi type="italic">it; and</hi> passing over he will preserve it. <div eID="gen16152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16153" type="x-p"/> This is the last of four chapters together that begin with woe; and they are all woes to the sinners that were found among the professing people of God, to the <hi type="italic">drunkards of Ephraim</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.28.1">ch. xxviii. 1</reference>), to <hi type="italic">Ariel</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.1">ch. xxix. 1</reference>), to the <hi type="italic">rebellious children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.30.1">ch. xxx. 1</reference>), and here to <hi type="italic">those that go down to Egypt for help;</hi> for men's relation to the church will not secure them from divine woes if they live in contempt of divine laws. Observe, <div eID="gen16153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> I. What the sin was that is here reproved, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. Idolizing the Egyptians, and making court to them, as if happy were the people that had the Egyptians for their friends and allies. They <hi type="italic">go down to Egypt for help</hi> in every exigence, as if the worshippers of false gods had a better interest in heaven and were more likely to have success of earth than the servants of the living and true God. That which invited them to Egypt was that the Egyptians had many chariots to accommodate them with, and horses and horsemen that were strong; and, if they could get a good body of forces thence into their service, they would think themselves able to deal with the king of Assyria and his numerous army. Their kings were forbidden to multiply horses and chariots, and were told of the folly of trusting to them (<reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Ps. xx. 7</reference>); but they think themselves wiser than their Bible. 2. Slighting the God of Israel: <hi type="italic">They look not to the Holy One of Israel,</hi> as if he were not worth taking notice of in this distress. They advise not with him, seek not his favour, nor are in any care to make him their friend. <div eID="gen16154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16155" type="x-p"/> II. The gross absurdity and folly of this sin. 1. They neglected one whom, if they would not hope in him, they had reason to fear. They do not seek the Lord, nor make their application to him, <hi type="italic">yet he also is wise,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.2">v. 2</reference>. They are solicitous to get the Egyptians into an alliance with them, because they have the reputation of a politic people; and is not God wise too? and would not infinite wisdom, engaged on their side, stand them in more stead than all the policies of Egypt? They are at the pains of going down to Egypt, a tedious journey, when they might have had better advice, and better help, by looking up to heaven, and would not. But, if they will not court God's wisdom to act for them, they shall find it act against them. He is wise, too wise for them to outwit, and he will bring evil upon those who thus affront him. He will not call back his words as men do (because they are fickle and foolish), but he <hi type="italic">will arise against the house of the evil-doers,</hi> this cabal of them that go down to Egypt; God will appear to their confusion, according to the word that he has spoken, and will oppose the help they think to bring in from the workers of iniquity. Some think the Egyptians made it one condition of their coming into an alliance with him that they should worship the gods of Egypt, and they consented to it, and therefore they are both called <hi type="italic">evil-doers</hi> and <hi type="italic">workers of iniquity.</hi> 2. They trusted to those who were unable to help them and would soon appear to be so, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">v. 3</reference>. Let them know that <hi type="italic">the Egyptians,</hi> whom they depend so much upon, <hi type="italic">are men and not God.</hi> As it is good for men to <hi type="italic">know themselves to be but men</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.9.20">Ps. ix. 20</reference>), so it is good for us to consider that those we love and trust to are but men. They therefore can do nothing without God, nothing against him, nothing in comparison with him. They are men, and therefore fickle and foolish, mutable and mortal, here to day and gone to morrow; they are men, and therefore let us not make gods of them, by making them our hope and confidence, and expecting that in them which is to be found in God only; they are not God, they cannot do that for us which God can do, and will, if we trust in him. Let us not then neglect him, to seek to them; let us not forsake the rock of ages for broken reeds, nor the fountain of living waters for broken cisterns. The Egyptians indeed have horses that are very strong; but <hi type="italic">they are flesh, and not spirit,</hi> and therefore, strong as they are, they may be wearied with a long march, and become unserviceable, or be wounded and slain in battle, and leave their riders to be ridden over. Every one knows this, that the Egyptians are not God and their horses are not spirit; but those that seek to them for help do not consider it, else they would not put such confidence in them. Sinners may be convicted of folly by the plainest and most self-evident truths, which they cannot deny, but will not believe. 3. They would certainly be ruined with the Egyptians they trusted in, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.3">v. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">When the Lord</hi> does but <hi type="italic">stretch out his hand</hi> how easily, how effectually, will he make them ashamed of their confidence in Egypt, and the Egyptians ashamed of the encouragement they gave them to trust in them; for <hi type="italic">he that helps and he that is helped shall fall together,</hi> and their mutual alliance shall prove their joint ruin. The Egyptians were shortly to be reckoned with, as appears by the <hi type="italic">burden of Egypt</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.1-Isa.19.25">ch. xix.</reference>), and then those who fled to them for shelter and succour should fall with them; for there is no escaping the judgments of God. <hi type="italic">Evil pursues sinners,</hi> and it is just with God to make that creature a scourge to us which we make an idol of. 4. They took God's work out of his hands. They pretended a great deal of care to preserve Jerusalem, in advising to an alliance with Egypt; and, when others would not fall in with their measures, they pleaded self preservation, and went to Egypt themselves. Now the prophet here tells them that Jerusalem should be preserved without aid from Egypt and that those who tarried there should be safe when those who fled to Egypt should be ruined. Jerusalem was under God's protection, and therefore there was no occasion to put it under the protection of Egypt. But a practical distrust of God's all-sufficiency is at the bottom of all our sinful departures from him to the creature. The prophet tells them he had it from God's own mouth: <hi type="italic">Thus hath the Lord spoken to me.</hi> They might depend upon it, (1.) That God would appear against Jerusalem's enemies with the boldness of a <hi type="italic">lion over his prey,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">v. 4</reference>. When the lion comes out to seize his prey <hi type="italic">a multitude of shepherds come out against him;</hi> for it becomes neighbours to help one another when persons or goods are in danger. These shepherds dare not come near the lion; all they can do is to make a <hi type="italic">noise,</hi> and with that they think to frighten him off. But does he regard it? <hi type="italic">No: he will not be afraid of their voice,</hi> nor abase himself so far as to be in the least moved by it either to quit his prey or to make any more haste than otherwise he would do in seizing it. <hi type="italic">Thus will the Lord of hosts come down to fight for Mount Zion,</hi> with such an unshaken undaunted resolution not to be moved by any opposition; and he will as easily and irresistibly destroy the Assyrian army as a lion tears a lamb in pieces. Whoever appear against God, they are but like a multitude of poor simple shepherds shouting at a lion, who scorns to take notice of them or so much as to alter his pace for them. Surely those that have such a protector need not go to Egypt for help. (2.) That God would appear for Jerusalem's friends with the tenderness of a bird over her young, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.5">v. 5</reference>. God was ready to <hi type="italic">gather Jerusalem, as a hen gathers her brood under her wings</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Matt. xxiii. 37</reference>); but those that trusted to the Egyptians would not be gathered. <hi type="italic">As birds flying</hi> to their nests with all possible speed, when they see them attacked, and fluttering about their nests with all possible concern, hovering over their young ones to protect them and drive away the assailants, with such compassion and affection <hi type="italic">will the Lord of hosts defend Jerusalem.</hi> As an eagle stirs up her young when they are in danger, <hi type="italic">takes them and bears them on her wings,</hi> so the Lord led Israel out of Egypt (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.11-Deut.32.12">Deut. xxxii. 11, 12</reference>); and he has now the same tender concern for them that he had then, so that they need not flee into Egypt again for shelter. <hi type="italic">Defending, he will deliver it;</hi> he will so defend it as to secure the continuance of its safety, not defend it for a while and abandon it at last, but defend it so that it shall not fall into the enemies' hand. <hi type="italic">I will defend this city to save it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.37.35">ch. xxxvii. 35</reference>. <hi type="italic">Passing over he will preserve it;</hi> the word for passing over is used in this sense only here and <reference osisRef="Exod.12.12">Exod. xii. 12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.23">23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.27">27</reference>, concerning the destroying angel's passing over the houses of the Israelites when he slew all the first-born of the Egyptians, to which story this passage refers. The Assyrian army was to be routed by a destroying angel, who should pass over Jerusalem, though that deserved to be destroyed, and draw his sword only against the besiegers. They shall be slain by the pestilence, but none of the besieged shall take the infection. Thus he will again pass over the houses of his people and secure them.
entries.462ab0a8b8323c93921932dc0fd937579259481a: <div eID="gen16155" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">A Call to Repentance; Deliverance of Jerusalem. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 720.)</title> <div sID="gen16156" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">6</hi> Turn ye unto <hi type="italic">him from</hi> whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted. <hi type="super">7</hi> For in that day every man shall cast away his idols of silver, and his idols of gold, which your own hands have made unto you <hi type="italic">for</hi> a sin. <hi type="super">8</hi> Then shall the Assyrian fall with the sword, not of a mighty man; and the sword, not of a mean man, shall devour him: but he shall flee from the sword, and his young men shall be discomfited. <hi type="super">9</hi> And he shall pass over to his strong hold for fear, and his princes shall be afraid of the ensign, saith the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , whose fire <hi type="italic">is</hi> in Zion, and his furnace in Jerusalem. <div eID="gen16156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16157" type="x-p"/> This explains the foregoing promise of the deliverance of Jerusalem; she shall be fitted for deliverance, and then it shall be wrought for her; for in that method God delivers. <div eID="gen16157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16158" type="x-p"/> I. Jerusalem shall be reformed, and so she shall be delivered from her enemies within her walls, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6-Isa.31.7">v. 6, 7</reference>. Here is, 1. A gracious call to repentance. This was the Lord's voice crying in the city, the voice of the rod, the voice of the sword, and the voice of the prophets interpreting the judgment: "<hi type="italic">Turn you,</hi> O turn you now, from your evil ways, <hi type="italic">unto God,</hi> return to your allegiance to him <hi type="italic">from whom the children of Israel have deeply revolted,</hi> from whom you, <hi type="italic">O children of Israel!</hi> have revolted." He reminds them of their birth and parentage, that they were <hi type="italic">children of Israel,</hi> and therefore under the highest obligations imaginable to the God of Israel, as an aggravation of their revolt from him and as an encouragement to them to return to him. "They have been backsliding children, yet children; therefore let them return, and their backslidings shall be healed. They have deeply revolted, with great address as they supposed (<hi type="italic">the revolters are profound,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.5.2">Hos. v. 2</reference>); but the issue will prove that they have revolted dangerously. The stain of their sins has gone deeply into their nature, not to be easily got out, like the blackness of the Ethiopian. <hi type="italic">They have deeply corrupted themselves</hi> (<reference osisRef="Hos.9.9">Hos. ix. 9</reference>); they have sunk deep into misery, and cannot easily recover themselves; therefore you have need to hasten your return to God." 2. A gracious promise of the good success of this call (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">In that day every man shall cast away his idols,</hi> in obedience to Hezekiah's orders, which, till they were alarmed by the Assyrian invasion, many refused to do. That is a happy fright which frightens us from our sins. (1.) It shall be a general reformation: every man shall cast away his own idols, shall begin with them before he undertakes to demolish other people's idols, which there will be no need of when every man reforms himself. (2.) It shall be a thorough reformation; for they shall part with their idolatry, their beloved sin, with their <hi type="italic">idols of silver and gold,</hi> their idols that they are most fond of. Many make an idol of their silver and gold, and by the love of that idol are drawn to revolt from God; but those that turn to God cast that away out of their hearts and will be ready to part with it when God calls. (3.) It shall be a reformation upon a right principle, a principle of piety, not of politics. They shall cast away their idols, because they have been unto them <hi type="italic">for a sin,</hi> an occasion of sin; therefore they will have nothing to do with them, though they had been the work of their <hi type="italic">own hands,</hi> and upon that account they had a particular fondness for them. Sin is the work of our own hands, but in working it we have been working our own ruin, and therefore we must cast it away; and those are strangely wedded to it who will not be prevailed upon to cast it away when they see that otherwise they themselves will be castaways. Some make this to be only a prediction that those who trust in idols, when they find they stand them in no stead, will cast them away in indignation. But it agrees so exactly with <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">ch. xxx. 22</reference> that I rather take it as a promise of a sincere reformation. <div eID="gen16158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen16159" type="x-p"/> II. Jerusalem's besiegers shall be routed, and so she shall be delivered from the enemies about her walls. The former makes way for this. If a people return to God, they may leave it to him to plead their cause against their enemies. When they have cast away their idols, <hi type="italic">then shall the Assyrian fall,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8-Isa.31.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. 1. The army of the Assyrians shall be laid dead upon the spot <hi type="italic">by the sword, not of a mighty man, nor of a mean man,</hi> not of any man at all, either Israelite or Egyptian, not forcibly by the sword of a mighty man nor surreptitiously by the sword of a mean man, but by the sword of an angel, who strikes more strongly than a mighty man and yet more secretly than a mean man, by the sword of the Lord, and his power and wrath in the hand of the angel. Thus the young men of the army shall melt, and be discomfited, and become tributaries to death. When God has work to do against the enemies of his church we expect it must be done by mighty men and mean men, officers and common soldiers; whereas God can, if he please, do it without either. <hi type="italic">He</hi> needs not armies of men who has legions of angels at command, <reference osisRef="Matt.26.53">Matt. xxvi. 53</reference>. 2. The king of Assyria shall flee for the same, shall flee from that invisible sword, hoping to get out of the reach of it; and he shall make the best of his way to his own dominions, shall pass over to some strong-hold of his own, for fear lest the Jews should pursue him now that his army was routed. Sennacherib had been very confident that he should make himself master of Jerusalem, and in the most insolent manner had set both God and Hezekiah at defiance; yet now he is made to tremble for fear of both. God can strike a terror into the proudest of men, and make the stoutest heart to tremble. See <reference osisRef="Job.18.11">Job xviii. 11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.20.24">xx. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">His princes</hi> that accompany him <hi type="italic">shall be afraid of the ensign,</hi> shall be in a continual fright at the remembrance of the ensign in the air, which perhaps the destroying angel displayed before he gave the fatal bow. Or they shall be afraid of every ensign they see, suspecting it is a party of the Jews pursuing them. The banner that God displays for the encouragement of his people (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.4">Ps. lx. 4</reference>) will be a terror to his and their enemies. Thus he <hi type="italic">cuts off the spirit of princes and is terrible to the kings of the earth.</hi> But who will do this? It is <hi type="italic">the Lord, whose fire is in Zion and his furnace in Jerusalem.</hi> (1.) Whose residence is there, and who there keeps house, as a man does where his fire and his oven are. It is the city of the great King, and let not the Assyrians think to turn him out of the possession of his own house. (2.) Who is there a consuming fire to all his enemies and will make them as a fiery oven in the day of his wrath, <reference osisRef="Ps.21.9">Ps. xxi. 9</reference>. He is himself <hi type="italic">a wall of fire round about Jerusalem,</hi> so that whoever assaults her does so at his peril, <reference osisRef="Zech.2.5">Zech. ii. 5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.11.5">Rev. xi. 5</reference>. (3.) Who has his altar there, on which the holy fire is continually kept burning and sacrifices are daily offered to his honour, and with which he is well pleased; and therefore he will defend this city, especially having an eye to the great sacrifice which was there also to be offered, of which all the sacrifices were types. If we keep up the fire of holy love and devotion in our hearts and houses, we may depend upon God to be a protection to us and them.  <chapter eID="Isa.31"/> <div eID="gen16159" type="x-p"/>

entries.fea3d6902bcdf27d924819051c3650f1d73e4f13: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8887"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 31</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Isa.31.1-Isa.31.9">Is 31:1-9</reference>. The Chief Strength of the Egyptian Armies Lay in Their Cavalry.</title> <div sID="gen14869" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8887"/><hi type="bold">1. and stay on horses, and trust in chariots--</hi>In their level and fertile plains horses could easily be used and fed (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.9">Ex 14:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.28">1Ki 10:28</reference>). In hilly Palestine horses were not so easily had or available. The Jews were therefore the more eager to get Egyptian chariots as allies against the Assyrian cavalry. In Assyrian sculptures chariots are represented drawn by three horses, and with three men in them (see <reference osisRef="Isa.36.9">Is 36:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.20.7">Psa 20:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.9.13">Da 9:13</reference>). <div eID="gen14869" type="x-p"/>
entries.ececba5e222084b0d090fe542b7087ce3742dbca: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8888"/><div sID="gen14870" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8888"/><hi type="bold">2. he also is wise--</hi>as well as the Egyptian priests, so famed for wisdom (<reference osisRef="Acts.7.22">Ac 7:22</reference>), but who are "fools" before Him (<reference osisRef="Isa.19.11">Is 19:11</reference>). He not only devises, but executes what He devises without "calling back His words" (<reference osisRef="Num.23.19">Nu 23:19</reference>).<div eID="gen14870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">home--</hi>the whole race.<div eID="gen14871" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14872" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">help--</hi>the Egyptian succor sought by the Jews. <div eID="gen14872" type="x-p"/>
entries.59d15d2d69033f9e9ed334fb46694b4d3c4b2bb2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8889"/><div sID="gen14873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8889"/><hi type="bold">3. not spirit--</hi>not of divine power (<reference osisRef="Ps.56.4">Psa 56:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.146.3">146:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.146.5">5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Zech.4.6">Zec 4:6</reference>).<div eID="gen14873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that helpeth--</hi>Egypt.<div eID="gen14874" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14875" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">holpen--</hi>Judah. <div eID="gen14875" type="x-p"/>

(<reference osisRef="Isa.42.13">Is 42:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.10">Ho 11:10</reference>).<div eID="gen14876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">roaring on--</hi>"growling over" his prey.<div eID="gen14877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">abase himself--</hi>be disheartened or frightened. <div eID="gen14878" type="x-p"/>
entries.56e340581da5eeb4f76f404b27949ab32fd3a250: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8891"/><div sID="gen14879" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8891"/>5. As in the image of "the lion," the point of comparison is the fearless might of Jehovah; so in that of the birds, it is His solicitous affection (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.11">De 32:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.91.4">Psa 91:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.23.37">Mt 23:37</reference>).<div eID="gen14879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">flying--</hi>Rather, "which defend" their young with their wings; "to fly" is a secondary meaning of the Hebrew word [Maurer]. "Hovering over" to protect their young [G. V. Smith].<div eID="gen14880" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14881" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">passing over--</hi>as the destroying angel passing over, so as to spare the blood-marked houses of the Israelites on the first passover (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.13">Ex 12:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.27">23, 27</reference>). He passed, or leaped forward [Lowth], to destroy the enemy and to spare His people. <div eID="gen14881" type="x-p"/>
entries.cb6142a8c2a0eb71a89c18c65872eb5ba83f90f5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8892"/><div sID="gen14882" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8892"/>6. The power and love of Jehovah, just mentioned, are the strongest incentives for returning to Him (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.62">Eze 16:62</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ezek.16.63">63</reference>; <reference osisRef="Hos.6.1">Ho 6:1</reference>).<div eID="gen14882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye ... Israel--</hi>The change of person marks that when they return to the Lord, He will address them in more direct terms of communion in the second person; so long as they were revolters, God speaks of them, as more at a distance, in the third person, rather than to them. <div eID="gen14883" type="x-p"/>

In the day of trial the idols will be found to render no help and will therefore be cast away. entries.ad4655f2bfcef6b0e71655f0a5c7b7589133de40: <div eID="gen27765" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen27766" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27767" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27767" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen27766" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen27768" type="x-p"/> The Jews again reproved for their confidence in Egypt, finely contrasted with their neglect of the power and protection of God, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1-Isa.31.3">Isa 31:1-3</reference>. Deliverance and protection are, notwithstanding, promised, expressed by two similes; the first remarkably lofty and poetical, the latter singularly beautiful and tender, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">Isa 31:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.5">Isa 31:5</reference>. Exhortation to repentance, joined with the prediction of a more reformed period, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6">Isa 31:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.7">Isa 31:7</reference>. This chapter concludes like the preceding, with a prophecy of the fall of Sennacherib, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8">Isa 31:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.9">Isa 31:9</reference>. <div eID="gen27768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27769" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen27769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27770" type="x-p"/> Wo to them that go down to Egypt - This is a reproof to the Israelites for forming an alliance with the Egyptians, and not trusting in the Lord. <div eID="gen27770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27771" type="x-p"/> And stay on horses "Who trust in horses" - For ועל veal, and upon, first twenty MSS. of Kennicott's, thirty of De Rossi's, one of my own, and the Septuagint, Arabic, and Vulgate, read על al, upon, without the conjunction, which disturbs the sense.

entries.ae25ae1321291c168718258d732ee91f3a5067c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen27773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27774" type="x-p"/> Like as the lion - This comparison is exactly in the spirit and manner, and very nearly approaching to the expression, of Homer. Βη ρ' ιμεν, ὡστε λεων ορεσιτροφος, ὁστ' επιδευης Δηρον εῃ κρειων, κελεται δε ἑ θυμος αγηνωρ, Μηλων πειρησοντα, και ες πυκινον δομον ελθειν· Ειπερ γαρ χ' εὑρῃσι παρ' αυτοψι βωτορας ανδρας Συν κυσι και δουρεσσι φυλασσοντας περι μηλα, Ου ρα τ' απειρητος μεμονε σταθμοιο διεσθαι. Αλλ' ὁγ' αῥ η ἡρπαξε μεταλμενος, ηε και αυτος Εβλητ' εν πρωτοισι θοης απο χειρος ακοντι. <div eID="gen27774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27775" type="x-p"/> Iliad 12:299. <div eID="gen27775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27776" type="x-p"/> As the bold lion, mountain-bred, now long <div eID="gen27776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27777" type="x-p"/> Famished, with courage and with hunger stung <div eID="gen27777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27778" type="x-p"/> Attempts the thronged fold: him nought appals, <div eID="gen27778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27779" type="x-p"/> Though dogs and armed shepherds stand in guard <div eID="gen27779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27780" type="x-p"/> Collected; he nathless undaunted springs <div eID="gen27780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27781" type="x-p"/> O'er the high fence, and rends the trembling prey; <div eID="gen27781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27782" type="x-p"/> Or, rushing onward, in his breast receives <div eID="gen27782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27783" type="x-p"/> The well-aimed spear. <div eID="gen27783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27784" type="x-p"/> Of metaphors, allegories, and comparisons of the Hebrew poets, in which the Divine nature and attributes are represented under images taken from brutes and other low objects; of their effect, their sublimity, and the causes of it; see De Sac. Poes. Heb., Praelect. 16 sub. fin.
entries.f7859bae54861436a7b775daec0973310e0f3611: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen27784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27785" type="x-p"/> Passing over "Leaping forward" - The generality of interpreters observe in this place an allusion to the deliverance which God vouchsafed to his people when he destroyed the first-born of the Egyptians, and exempted those of the Israelites sojourning among them by a peculiar interposition. The same word is made use of here which is used upon that occasion, and which gave the name to the feast which was instituted in commemoration of that deliverance, פסח pesach. But the difficulty is to reconcile the commonly received meaning of that word with the circumstances of the similitude here used to illustrate the deliverance represented as parallel to the deliverance in Egypt. "As the mother birds hovering over their young, <div eID="gen27785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27786" type="x-p"/> So shall Jehovah God of hosts protect Jerusalem; <div eID="gen27786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27787" type="x-p"/> Protecting and delivering, passing over, and rescuing her." <div eID="gen27787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27788" type="x-p"/> This difficulty is, I think, well solved by Vitringa, whose remark is the more worthy of observation, as it leads to the true meaning of an important word, which hitherto seems greatly to have been misunderstood, though Vitringa himself, as it appears to me, has not exactly enough defined the precise meaning of it. He says, "פסח pasach signifies to cover, to protect by covering: σκεπασω ὑμας, Septuagint. Jehovah obteget ostium; 'The Lord will cover or protect the door:'" whereas it means that particular action or motion by which God at that time placed himself in such a situation as to protect the house of the Israelite against the destroying angel; to spring forward, to throw one's self in the way, in order to cover and protect. Cocceius comes nearer to the true meaning than Vitringa, by rendering it gradum facere, to march, to step forward; Lexicon in voc. The common meaning of the word פסח pasach upon other occasions is to halt, to be lame, to leap, as in a rude manner of dancing, (as the prophets of Baal did, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.26">1Kgs 18:26</reference>), all which agrees very well together; for the motion of a lame person is a perpetual springing forward, by throwing himself from the weaker upon the stronger leg. The common notion of God's passage over the houses of the Israelites is, that in going through the land of Egypt to smite the first-born, seeing the blood on the door of the houses of the Israelites, he passed over, or skipped, those houses, and forbore to smite them. But that this is not the true notion of the thing, will be plain from considering the words of the sacred historian, where he describes very explicitly the action: "For Jehovah will pass through to smite the Egyptians; and when he seeth the blood on the lintels and on the two side posts, Jehovah will spring forward over (or before) the door, ופסח יהוה על הפתח upasach Yehovah al happethach, and will not suffer the destroyer to come into your houses to smite you, "<reference osisRef="Exo.12.23">Exo 12:23</reference>. Here are manifestly two distinct agents, with which the notion of passing over is not consistent, for that supposes but one agent. The two agents are the destroying angel passing through to smite every house, and Jehovah the Protector keeping pace with him; and who, seeing the door of the Israelite marked with the blood, the token prescribed, leaps forward, throws himself with a sudden motion in the way, opposes the destroying angel, and covers and protects that house against the destroying angel, nor suffers him to smite it. In this way of considering the action, the beautiful similitude of the bird protecting her young answers exactly to the application by the allusion to the deliverance in Egypt. As the mother bird spreads her wings to cover her young, throws herself before them, and opposes the rapacious bird that assaults them, so shall Jehovah protect, as with a shield, Jerusalem from the enemy, protecting and delivering, springing forward and rescuing her; ὑπερβαινων, as the three other Greek interpreters, Aquila, Symmachus, and Theodotion, render it. The Septuagint, περιποιησεται· instead of which MS. Pachom. has περιβησεται, circumeundo proteget, "in going about he shall protect, "which I think is the true reading. - Homer, 2 viii. 329, expresses the very same image by this word: - Αιας δ' ουκ αμελησε κασιγνητοιο πεσοντος, Αλλα θεων περιβη, και οἱ σακος αμφεκαλυψε: " - But Ajax his broad shield displayed, <div eID="gen27788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27789" type="x-p"/> And screened his brother with a mighty shade." - Ὁς Χρυσην αμφιβεβηκας. <div eID="gen27789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27790" type="x-p"/> Il. 1:37 <div eID="gen27790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27791" type="x-p"/> Which the scholiast explains by περιβεβηκας, ὑπερμαχεις, i.e., "Thou who strictly guardest Chryses." - L. On this verse Kimchi says, "The angel of the Lord which destroyed the Assyrians is compared to a lion, <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">Isa 31:4</reference>, for his strength: and here (<reference osisRef="Isa.31.5">Isa 31:5</reference>) to flying birds, for his swiftness."
entries.b96b3630be6e2fd3a54852b1a6ae48408839c2fd: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen27791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27792" type="x-p"/> Have deeply revolted "Have so deeply engaged in revolt" - All the ancient Versions read תעמיקו taamiku, in the second person, instead of העמיקו heemiku, they have deeply revolted, etc.
entries.e492e3ba3038e7b6298719e413116c983af31c7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen27792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27793" type="x-p"/> Which your own hands have made unto you for a sin "The sin, which their own hands have made" - The construction of the word חטא chet, sin, in this place is not easy. The Septuagint have omitted it: MSS. Pachom. and 1. D. 2 and Cod. Marchal. in margine, supply the omission by the word ἁμαρτιαν, sin, or ἁμαρτημα, said to be from Aquila's Version, which I have followed. The learned Professor Schroeder, Institut. Ling. Hebrews p. 298, makes it to be in regimine with ידיכם yedeychem, as an epithet, your sinful hands. The Septuagint render the pronoun in the third person, αἱ χειρες αυτων, their hands; and an ancient MS. has, agreeable to that rendering, להם lahem, to them, for לכם lachem, to you; which word they have likewise omitted, as not necessary to complete the sense.
entries.cacdc8d55668be990f4deb4fa989d1fc7a9d5149: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen27793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen27794" type="x-p"/> Then shall the Assyrian fall, etc. - Because he was to be discomfited by the angel of the Lord, destroying in his camp, in one night, upwards of one hundred and eighty thousand men; and Sennacherib himself fell by the hands of the princes, his own sons. Not mighty men, for they were not soldiers; not mean men, for they were princes.  <chapter eID="Isa.31"/> <div eID="gen27794" type="x-p"/>

entries.89d63ff9424840007fe615d9515461da35b5ccd9: <reference osisRef="Isa.31.1-Isa.31.3">Isa 31:1-3</reference> <div eID="gen13199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13200" type="x-p"/> There is nothing to surprise us in the fact, that the prophet returns again and again to the alliance with Egypt. After his warning had failed to prevent it, he wrestled with it in spirit, set before himself afresh the curse which would be its certain fruit, brought out and unfolded the consolation of believers that lay hidden in the curse, and did not rest till the cursed fruit, that had become a real thing, had been swallowed up by the promise, which was equally real. The situation of this fourth woe is just the same as that of the previous one. The alliance with Egypt is still in progress. <hi type="italic">“Woe to them that go down to Egypt for help, and rely upon horses, and put their trust in chariots, that there are many of them; and in horsemen, that there is a powerful multitude of them; and do not look up to the Holy One of Israel, and do not inquire for Jehovah! And yet He also is wise; thus then He brings evil, and sets not His words aside; and rises up against the house of miscreants, and against the help of evil-doers. And Egypt is man, and not God; and its horses flesh, and not spirit. And when Jehovah stretches out His hand, the helper stumbles, and he that is helped falls, and they all perish together.”</hi> The expression “them that go down” (<hi type="italic">hayyōredı̄m</hi>) does not imply that the going down was taking place just then for the first time. It is the participle of qualification, just as God is called הבּרא. לעזרה with <hi type="italic">Lamed</hi> of the object, as in Isa 20:6. The horses, chariots, and horsemen here, as those of Egypt, which Diodorus calls ἱππάσιμος, on account of its soil being so suitable for cavalry (see Lepsius in Herzog’s <hi type="italic">Cyclopaedia</hi>). The participle is combined in the finite verb. Instead of ועל־סוּסים, we also find the reading preferred by Norzi, of על without <hi type="italic">Vav</hi>, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.5.11">Isa 5:11</reference> (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.5.23">Isa 5:23</reference>). The perfects, שׁעוּ לא and דרשׁוּ לא, are used without any definite time, to denote that which was always wanting in them. The circumstantial clause, “whilst He is assuredly also wise,” i.e., will bear comparison with their wisdom and that of Egypt, is a touching μείωσις. It was not necessary to think very highly of Jehovah, in order to perceive the reprehensible and destructive character of their apostasy from Him. The fut. consec. ויּבא is used to indicate the inevitable consequence of their despising Him who is also wise. He will not set aside His threatening words, but carry them out. The house of miscreants is Judah (<reference osisRef="Isa.1.4">Isa 1:4</reference>); and the help (<hi type="italic">abstr. pro concr.</hi>, just as Jehovah is frequently called “my help,” <hi type="italic">‛ezrâthı̄</hi>, by the Psalmist) of evil-doers is Egypt, whose help has been sought by Judah. The latter is “man” (<hi type="italic">'âdâm</hi>), and its horses “flesh” (<hi type="italic">bâsâr</hi>); whereas Jehovah is God (<hi type="italic">El</hi>) and spirit (<hi type="italic">rūăch</hi>; see <hi type="italic">Psychol.</hi> p. 85). Hofmann expounds it correctly: “As ruuach has life in itself, it is opposed to the <hi type="italic">bâsâr</hi>, which is only rendered living through the <hi type="italic">rūăch</hi>; and so <hi type="italic">El</hi> is opposed to the corporeal <hi type="italic">'âdâm</hi>, who needs the spirit in order to live at all.” Thus have they preferred the help of the impotent and conditioned, to the help of the almighty and all-conditioning One. Jehovah, who is God and spirit, only requires to stretch out His hand (an anthropomorphism, by the side of which we find the rule for interpreting it); and the helpers, and those who are helped (i.e., according to the terms of the treaty, though not in reality), that is to say, both the source of the help and the object of help, are all cast into one heap together.
entries.a13cc9ff681450cb0e69270f3aed2a59d796b169: <reference osisRef="Isa.31.4">Isa 31:4</reference> <div eID="gen13200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13201" type="x-p"/> And things of this kind would occur. <hi type="italic">“For thus hath Jehovah spoken to me, As the lion growls, and the young lion over its prey, against which a whole crowd of shepherds is called together; he is not alarmed at their cry, and does not surrender at their noise; so will Jehovah of hosts descend to the campaign against the mountain of Zion, and against their hill.”</hi> There is no other passage in the book of Isaiah which sounds so Homeric as this (vid., <hi type="italic">Il</hi>. xviii. 161, 162, xii. 299ff.). It has been misunderstood by Knobel, Umbreit, Drechsler, and others, who suppose על לצבּא to refer to Jehovah’s purpose to fight for Jerusalem: Jehovah, who would no more allow His city to be taken from Him, than a lion would give up a lamb that it had taken as its prey. But how could Jerusalem be compared to a lamb which a lion holds in its claws as <hi type="italic">tereph</hi>? (<reference osisRef="Isa.5.29">Isa 5:29</reference>). We may see, even from <reference osisRef="Isa.29.7">Isa 29:7</reference>, what construction is meant to be put upon על צבא. Those sinners and their protectors would first of all perish; for like a fierce indomitable lion would Jehovah advance against Jerusalem, and take it as His prey, without suffering Himself to be thwarted by the Judaeans and Egyptians, who set themselves in opposition to His army (The Assyrians). The mountain of Zion was the citadel and temple; the hill of Zion the city of Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.10.32">Isa 10:32</reference>). They would both be given up to the judgment of Jehovah, without any possibility of escape. The commentators have been misled by the fact, that a simile of a promising character follows immediately afterwards, without anything to connect the one with the other. But this abrupt μετάβασις was intended as a surprise, and was a true picture of the actual fulfilment of the prophecy; for in the moment of the greatest distress, when the actual existence of Jerusalem was in question (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.10.33-Isa.10.34">Isa 10:33-34</reference>), the fate of Ariel took suddenly and miraculously a totally different turn (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.2">Isa 29:2</reference>). In this sense, a pleasant picture is placed side by side with the terrible one (compare Mic 5:6-7).
entries.7e396b56435ccac0d9431eb7f02885b84c947485: <reference osisRef="Isa.31.5">Isa 31:5</reference> <div eID="gen13201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13202" type="x-p"/> Jehovah suddenly arrests the work of punishment, and the love which the wrath enfolds within itself begins to appear. <hi type="italic">“Like fluttering birds, so will Jehovah of Hosts screen Jerusalem; screening and delivering, sparing and setting free.”</hi> The prophet uses the plural, “like fluttering birds,” with an object - namely, not so much to represent Jehovah Himself, as the tender care and, as it were, <hi type="italic">maternal</hi> love, into which His leonine fierceness would be changed. This is indicated by the fact, that he attaches the feminine <hi type="italic">‛âphōth</hi> to the common gender <hi type="italic">tsippŏrı̄m</hi>. The word <hi type="italic">pâsōăch</hi> recals to mind the deliverance from Egypt (as in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.29">Isa 30:29</reference>) in a very significant manner. The sparing of the Israelites by the destroyer passing over their doors, from which the passover derived its name, would be repeated once more. We may see from this, that in and along with Assyria, Jehovah Himself, whose instrument of punishment Assyria was, would take the filed against Jerusalem (<reference osisRef="Isa.29.2-Isa.29.3">Isa 29:2-3</reference>); but His attitude towards Jerusalem is suddenly changed into one resembling the action of birds, as they soar round and above their threatened nests. On the inf. abs. <hi type="italic">kal</hi> (<hi type="italic">gânōn</hi>) after the <hi type="italic">hiphil</hi>, see Ewald, §312, <hi type="italic">b</hi>; and on the continuance of the inf. abs. in the finite verb, §350, a. This generally takes place through the future, but here through the preterite, as in <reference osisRef="Jer.23.14">Jer 23:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.26.13">Gen 26:13</reference>, and <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.26">1Sa 2:26</reference> (if indeed <hi type="italic">vegâdēl</hi> is the third pers. preterite there).
entries.e9e14894d446158f60982089af3ecd35bfc936a8: <reference osisRef="Isa.31.6">Isa 31:6</reference> <div eID="gen13202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13203" type="x-p"/> On the ground of this half terrible, half comforting picture of the future, the call to repentance is now addressed to the people of the prophet’s own time. <hi type="italic">“Then turn, O sons of Israel, to Him from whom men have so deeply departed.”</hi> Strictly speaking, “to Him with regard to whom (אשׁר) ye are deeply fallen away” (<hi type="italic">he‛ĕmı̄q</hi>, as in Hos 9:9, and <hi type="italic">sârâh</hi>, that which is alienated, alienation, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.1.5">Isa 1:5</reference>); the transition to the third person is like the reverse in Isa 1:29. This call to repentance the prophet strengthens by two powerful motives drawn from the future.
entries.75c59c98ed4e47a50ce2e6ba91eb9166134a216e: <reference osisRef="Isa.31.7">Isa 31:7</reference> <div eID="gen13203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13204" type="x-p"/> The first is, that idolatry would one day be recognised in all its abomination, and put away. <hi type="italic">“For in that day they will abhor every one their silver idols and their gold idols, which your hands have made you for a sin,”</hi> i.e., to commit sin and repent, with the preponderance of the latter idea, as in <hi type="italic">Hos 8:11</hi> (compare 1Ki 13:34). חטא, a second accusative to עשׂוּ, indicating the result. The prospect is the same as that held out in <reference osisRef="Isa.30.22">Isa 30:22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.27.9">Isa 27:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.17.8">Isa 17:8</reference>; Isa 2:20.
entries.f2db1b6234620a3a51b8ed39d8d2cbfe3aac2062: <reference osisRef="Isa.31.8-Isa.31.9">Isa 31:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen13204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen13205" type="x-p"/> The second motive is, that Israel will not be rescued by men, but by Jehovah alone; so that even He from whom they have now so deeply fallen will prove Himself the only true ground of confidence. <hi type="italic">“And Asshur falls by a sword not of a man, and a sword not of a man will devour him; and he flees before a sword, and his young men become tributary. And his rock, for fear will it pass away, and his princes be frightened away by the flags: the saying of Jehovah, who has His fire in Zion, and His furnace in Jerusalem.”</hi> The lxx and Jerome render this falsely φεύξεται οὐκ (לא) ἀπὸ προσώπου μαχαίρας. לו is an ethical dative, and the prophet intentionally writes “before a sword” without any article, to suggest the idea of the unbounded, infinite, awful (cf., <reference osisRef="Isa.28.2">Isa 28:2</reference>, <hi type="italic">beyâd</hi>; <hi type="italic">Psalter</hi>, vol. i. p. 15). A sword is drawn without any human intervention, and before this Asshur falls, or at least so many of the Assyrians as are unable to save themselves by flight. The power of Asshur is for ever broken; even its young men will henceforth become tributary, or perform feudal service. By “his rock” most commentators understand the rock upon which the fugitive would gladly have taken refuge, but did not dare (Rosenmüller, Gesenius, Knobel, etc.); others, again, the military force of Asshur, as its supposed invincible refuge (Saad., etc.); others, the apparently indestructible might of Asshur generally (Vulgate, Rashi, Hitzig). But the presence of “his princes” in the parallel clause makes it most natural to refer “his rock” to the king; and this reference is established with certainty by what <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa 32:2</reference> affirms of the king and princes of Judah. Luther also renders it thus: <hi type="italic">und jr Fels wird fur furcht wegzihen</hi> (and their rock will withdraw for fear). Sennacherib really did hurry back to Assyria after the catastrophe in a most rapid flight. <hi type="italic">Minnēs</hi> are the standards of Asshur, which the commanders of the army fly away from in terror, without attempting to rally those that were scattered. Thus speaks Jehovah, and this is what He decrees who has His <hi type="italic">'ūr</hi> and <hi type="italic">tannūr</hi> in Jerusalem. We cannot suppose that the allusion here is to the fire and hearth of the sacrifices; for <hi type="italic">tannūr</hi> does not mean a hearth, but a furnace (from <hi type="italic">nūr</hi>, to burn). The reference is to the light of the divine presence, which was outwardly a devouring fire for the enemies of Jerusalem, an unapproachable red-hot furnace (<hi type="italic">ignis et caminus qui devorat peccatores et ligna, faenum stipulamque consumit</hi>: Jerome).  <chapter eID="Isa.31"/> <div eID="gen13205" type="x-p"/>

entries.1e40df4606c5643eca8142cdbc1242f6451371cb: <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.31.1" annotateType="commentary" osisID="Isa.31.1" sID="gen45604" type="section"/> <div sID="gen45605" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">1.</hi> <hi type="italic">Woe to them that go down to Egypt.</hi> He again returns to the subject which he had handled at the beginning of the former chapter; for he still cries loudly against the Jews, whose ordinary custom it was, in seasons of danger, to resort, not to the Lord, but to the Egyptians. We have formerly explained why this was so highly displeasing to God. To state the matter briefly, there are two reasons why the Prophet reproves this crime so severely. The first is, because it is impossible for us to place confidence for our salvation in creatures, and at the same time in God; for our eyes must be withdrawn from him as soon as they are directed to them. The second reason is, God had expressly forbidden them to enter into alliance with the Egyptians. (<reference osisRef="Bible:Deut.17.16">Deuteronomy 17:16</reference>.) To sinful confidence was added rebelliousness, as if they had resolved to provide for their safety by despising God, and by disobeying his will.<div eID="gen45605" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45606" type="x-p"/>We must therefore look at the source of this evil, if we wish to understand fully the Prophet’s meaning. There was also a peculiar reason, as we have formerly remarked, why the Lord wished the Jews to have no intercourse with the Egyptians. It was, lest that wicked alliance should obliterate the remembrance of the redemption from Egypt, and lest they should be corrupted by the superstitions and sinful idolatry of the Egyptians. Yet these arguments were regarded by them as of no weight; and, though God had forbidden it, this did not hinder them from continually applying to them for assistance, and imagining that their assistance was a shield which defended them against the arm of God. Consequently, there are good reasons why the Prophet exclaims so earnestly against such madness. Even on the ground that God had forbidden it, their “going down into Egypt” deserved to be severely blamed; but it was still more intolerably criminal, that by false confidence they bestowed on mortal men the glory which was due to God. In order to make it still more clear that in this manner they defraud God of his right, he not only accuses them of having relied on the Egyptians, but likewise brings a charge against them, on the other hand, that<div eID="gen45606" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45607" type="x-p"/><hi type="italic">They have not looked to the Holy One of Israel.</hi> Here appears more clearly the reason why that treachery of the Jews is so sharply reproved by Isaiah; for in other respects God does not disapprove of our using lawful remedies, just as we eat bread and other kinds of food which were intended for our use. Thus if any person, placed in danger, employ means which were not forbidden, but which are customary and lawful, provided that he do not at all deny the power of God, he certainly ought not to be blamed; but if we are so strongly attached to outward means, that we do not at the same time seek God, and if, through distrust of his promises, we resort to unlawful methods, this is worthy of condemnation and abhorrence.<div eID="gen45607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45608" type="x-p"/>The word <hi type="italic">look</hi> is frequently employed in Scripture to denote this confidence; for we commonly turn our eyes towards that quarter from which we expect assistance. In a word, we are here taught that we ought to place our trust for salvation in none other than in God alone, that, relying on his promises, we may boldly ask from him whatever is desirable. He undoubtedly permits us to use all things which he intended for our use, but in such a manner that our minds must be entirely fixed on him.<div eID="gen45608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen45609" type="x-p"/>When he calls God “the Holy One of Israel,” he presents in a striking light the wickedness and ingratitude of the people, who, after having been taken under God’s protection and guardianship, despised such a protector and guardian of their salvation, and ran eagerly after their own lusts. By immediately adding, <hi type="italic">neither have they sought Jehovah,</hi> he shews that neither the power, nor the goodness, nor the fatherly kindness of God, could keep them in the discharge of their duty. In the present day, since he invites us not less kindly to come to him, we offer a grievous insult to him if we look to any other, and do not resolve to trust in him alone; and everything that shall turn away and withdraw our minds from God will be to us like “Egypt.”<div eID="gen45609" type="x-p"/> <div annotateRef="Bible:Isa.31.1" annotateType="commentary" eID="gen45604" osisID="Isa.31.1" type="section"/>
